sources.title: George Gershwin (Q123829) -- verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-16): English label 'George Gershwin', description 'American composer and pianist (1898-1937)', Korean label present, instance of human, born 26 September 1898, died 11 July 1937, citizenship United States. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Raymond A. White (curator of the George and Ira Gershwin Collection), 'The Gershwin Legacy: Library Celebrates Contributions of George and Ira', Library of Congress Information Bulletin, September 1998 -- CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: the Library's curator calls Gershwin one of America's most important composers who, alone and with his brother Ira, wrote many of the finest American popular songs and orchestral pieces, names the Library's Music Division the premier institution for Gershwin studies and its collection the world's preeminent body of primary sources on the brothers, and describes the holdings: the full score of Porgy and Bess (which he says conveys Gershwin's care in making the opera and the importance he attached to it), the manuscripts of Rhapsody in Blue, An American in Paris, Concerto in F and Porgy and Bess given in 1953 from their mother's estate, song manuscripts with erasures and corrections, his harmony exercises and eight sketchbooks, scrapbooks (seven devoted to Porgy and Bess) and the Theatre Guild's Porgy and Bess files. Institutional article by the collection's own curator, admiring but factual in tone. Read in full.

Helen Dalrymple, ''S Wonderful: The Gershwins Come Alive in Symposium', Library of Congress Information Bulletin, April 1998 -- the Library's report on its March 1998 symposium 'The Gershwins and Their World' (the opening of the George and Ira Gershwin Room): pianist and historian Artis Wodehouse on the 140 piano rolls Gershwin made between 1915 and 1925 and the influence of black and Spanish rhythms on them; the original Bess, Anne Wiggins Brown, on her audition for him and the 1935 production; the composer David Raksin and other speakers on how much George enjoyed helping young musicians; and sessions on his 1928 meeting with Alban Berg in Paris and on other musical influences. Press-office report of other people's recollections and papers, with friends and relatives among the speakers and admiring in tone; used only as supporting evidence. Read in full; the passage on a Washington theatre's whites-only audience policy was not used (an audience-access dispute, politics-adjacent and unscored).

Jim Farrington (Head of Public Services, Sibley Music Library, Eastman School of Music; guest essay), ''Rhapsody in Blue'--George Gershwin, piano; Paul Whiteman Orchestra (1924)', Library of Congress National Recording Registry essay (added to the Registry in 2002) -- an independent librarian-scholar's essay hosted by the Library: a 4 January 1924 New York Tribune item announcing a 'jazz concerto' by Gershwin for Paul Whiteman's 12 February concert 'An Experiment in Modern Music' at Aeolian Hall, a commission that had slipped his mind while he worked on a Broadway musical; the rushed schedule and Whiteman's arranger Ferde Grofe orchestrating from Gershwin's two-piano score page by page as it was finished; the clarinet glissando that Ross Gorman improvised in rehearsal, to Gershwin's delight; the mixed press, quoting Lawrence Gilman's hostile New York Tribune notice (which still concedes the 'rich inventiveness of the rhythms') and Leonard Bernstein's 1955 verdict that the Rhapsody is a string of separate paragraphs with inspired themes; the 1924 and 1927 recordings, the essay's finding that the million-seller claim is unsupported, and Gershwin's unhappiness with Whiteman's conducting in 1927 (Nathaniel Shilkret conducted instead). It calls the work arguably the most famous piece of American classical music ever written. Independent, with a hostile voice and a mixed verdict; the views are the author's, as the Library's own disclaimer says. Read in full.

University of Michigan School of Music, Theatre & Dance, 'Gershwin Centennial Celebration' concert program, 26 January 2025 (program notes by the editors of the George and Ira Gershwin Critical Edition, including Timothy Freeze, volume editor, on the Concerto in F) -- scholarly notes on the brothers' 1924-25 seasons: four Gershwin shows opening in 1924, the most of any year of his life, and three musicals plus the Concerto in F in 1925; Walter Damrosch's April 1925 commission to compose, orchestrate and perform a piano concerto for the New York Symphony Society; the 3 December 1925 Carnegie Hall premiere as Gershwin's debut as pianist, composer and creator of score-oriented works, since in his earlier music he had supplied only the basic musical shape for singers, arrangers and producers to adapt and Rhapsody in Blue was arranged by Ferde Grofe; the Concerto as the first major work he orchestrated, as he did all his later concert works and Porgy and Bess; the editor's finding that his manuscripts show impatience with notating fine detail (pitches and rhythms careful, tempo, articulation and dynamics inconsistent) and that he routinely modified details in later performances; and Ira's crucial contributions to Porgy and Bess. Scholarly editors working with the Gershwin estates: admiring of the music but critical of the manuscripts. Read the introduction and the Concerto in F note in full; the rest of the program (notes on Ira, on Robert Russell Bennett and on the other 1925 shows) was searched by keyword only.

University of Michigan News, 'U-M to become epicenter of research on music of George & Ira Gershwin', 14 September 2013 -- the university's release announcing its partnership with the Gershwin estates to prepare the first critical edition of the works (the Gershwin Initiative): it lists the works to be edited (Porgy and Bess, Rhapsody in Blue, An American in Paris, Concerto in F, Cuban Overture and scores the brothers wrote for more than two dozen Broadway and Hollywood musicals), says the scores of Porgy and Bess and Rhapsody in Blue circulate in problematic editions, and has project leaders describe the music as lying at the crossroads of blues, jazz, popular song, the Broadway stage and the Western European tradition. Institutional promotional release with quotations from the estates' trustees (promotional; their superlatives are not repeated as fact); the sentence on his death was not used. Read in full.

David Zax, 'Summertime for George Gershwin', Smithsonian Institution's Air & Space magazine website (a Smithsonian-magazine feature; the page shows no publication date) -- a feature drawing on Gershwin's letters, DuBose Heyward's recollections and biographers: Gershwin read the novel Porgy in 1926 and wrote to Heyward about setting it; Heyward insisted on fieldwork among the Gullah community of the Charleston area; short stops in Charleston in December 1933 and January 1934 and a New York Herald Tribune report that he had become an eager student of Negro music; the June 1934 stay on Folly Island, with Heyward taking him to the schools and churches of neighbouring James Island to hear spirituals and the dance called shouting; slow progress over the winter and spring followed by several months of heightened productivity; contemporary critics divided and a disappointingly brief first run; the Metropolitan Opera repertory in 1985; and the long debate over the opera's treatment of race (Harry Belafonte and Sidney Poitier declining the 1959 film). Journalistic feature with a non-hagiographic tone. Read in full; the passages on his social life, courtship and holiday habits were not used, nor was a linked article about a supposed attention disorder, and a July trip to a cabin church service (placed in North Carolina in the text, unlike the rest of the trip) was not used.

Joseph Horowitz, 'The Gershwin Moment (continued)', josephhorowitz.com (the post reprints the author's review of Larry Starr's George Gershwin, Yale University Press, written for the Times Literary Supplement; the page shows no date) -- a cultural historian's essay-review that gathers judgments of Gershwin: Arnold Schoenberg's eulogy, Jascha Heifetz's remarks and recordings, Fritz Reiner's Porgy and Bess synthesis, Ravel and Shostakovich on one side, and on the other the tone of American critics (Aaron Copland's 1937 remark that Gershwin was serious up to a point, Virgil Thomson's review of Porgy and Bess as crooked folklore and halfway opera, a dismissive 1980 New Grove entry); and Starr's argument that Gershwin never evinced a divided allegiance between art and popular music, with Ira Gershwin's remark that George wrote some of his best hits after the Great American Opera. Advocate's essay (the author champions a new Gershwin), used for its record of the counter-voices and for the range claim, never alone; a critic's prejudiced remark about Jewish immigrants quoted in it was not used. Read in full.

Edward Morrow, 'Duke Ellington on Gershwin's "Porgy"', New Theatre, vol. 2 no. 12, December 1935 (reprinted at Revolution's Newsstand, 27 May 2023) -- a 1935 interview in which Duke Ellington, then an established bandleader and composer, gives his view of Porgy and Bess: grand music, but not fitting the mood and spirit of the story and not using the Negro musical idiom, borrowing from everyone from Liszt to a kazoo band, with the hurricane passages as the one place the music worked and the characterisation weak elsewhere; he also claims, unverified, that passages of Rhapsody in Blue came from an earlier song. A peer composer's critique of the work and the strongest counter-voice read. It appeared in a Communist Party-supported magazine whose interviewer adds his own political commentary, including the phrase 'lamp-black Negroisms', which in the reprinted text is the interviewer's wording and not Ellington's; that framing is not used or scored. Read in full.

Arnold Schoenberg Center, Vienna, 'VR05: Tribute to George Gershwin' (spoken tribute recorded 12 July 1937, with the Center's transcription) -- a one-minute tribute on Gershwin's death: music was for him the air he breathed, he was a great composer whose work benefited a national American music and also contributed to the music of the whole world, and Schoenberg lost a friend. A peer composer's tribute on his death, admiring and retrospective, about his music and not his conduct. Read in full (about 100 words).

Kennedy Center, 'George Gershwin' artist biography -- the national performing-arts centre's short biography: Tin Pan Alley song plugger and piano-roll maker, first big hit Swanee (1917), twenty-two Broadway shows with Ira and other lyricists in the 1920s and early 1930s, the concert works commissioned through Paul Whiteman (Rhapsody in Blue, 1924) and Walter Damrosch (the piano concerto, 1925), An American in Paris (1928), Porgy and Bess written with Ira and DuBose and Dorothy Heyward and received with mixed reviews, and film scores for Fred Astaire after Porgy and Bess. Institutional biography, neutral in tone; its sentence saying that Whiteman's concerts first presented An American in Paris was not used (the premiere is not described in the other sources read) and the passages on his illness and death were not used. Read in full.

New York Public Library Archives & Manuscripts, 'Joseph Schillinger papers' finding aid (biographical note and scope-and-arrangement text) -- the library's finding aid for the theorist and teacher's papers: Schillinger taught a system of composition that reduced musical elements, rhythm in particular, to mathematical relationships; his students included George Gershwin, Tommy Dorsey and Oscar Levant; the papers include extensive correspondence with students, with Gershwin's correspondence held by the Library of Congress and reproductions of Gershwin letters in the correspondence series. Archival description, neutral; it confirms the teacher-student relationship but gives no dates or content of the lessons, and the container list was not read.

Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, item record 2005678096, '[George Gershwin, 1898-1937, half-length portrait, standing, facing left]' (George Grantham Bain Collection; 1 photographic print; call number BIOG FILE [item] [P&P]; reproduction number LC-USZ62-60866) -- checked for the portrait's rights: the record gives the Rights Advisory 'No known restrictions on publication', notes 'Photo by Bain News Service', says it 'contains unverified, old data from caption card' and records no date; the Library's Prints & Photographs rights statement for the Bain collection (read from its rights-statements research guide, last revised November 2015) says there are no known copyright restrictions on the photographs in the George Grantham Bain Collection and that publicity rights may apply, with the credit line 'Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division' plus the reproduction number. The record was read through the Library's JSON interface and the master TIFF (1177 x 1536 pixels) downloaded from the Library's storage service. Not used for any scoring.

Wikimedia Commons file page 'George Gershwin, 1898-1937, half-length portrait, standing, facing left LCCN2005678096.jpg' -- checked through the Commons API (file metadata and categories) for the portrait's file and licence tags: George Grantham Bain Collection, from the Library of Congress (digital ID cph.3a42852), uploaded 2018, 1177 x 1536 pixels, tagged public domain (PD-Bain, 'PD US no notice', 'Library of Congress - no known copyright restrictions'), with the tag's own note that it does not by itself indicate copyright status. Not used for any scoring.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_gershwin_loc_white, src_gershwin_umich_news, src_gershwin_umich_freeze, src_gershwin_loc_nrr, src_gershwin_kennedy, src_gershwin_horowitz | 1919-1937 | Library of Congress curator + university release + critical-edition notes + Registry essay + Kennedy Center biography + essay-review] The Library's curator describes popular songs and orchestral pieces and holds his manuscripts for Broadway shows, concert works and the opera; Michigan lists the works under edition as scores for more than two dozen Broadway and Hollywood musicals plus Rhapsody in Blue, An American in Paris, the Concerto in F and Porgy and Bess, and its project leaders place the music where blues, jazz, popular song, the Broadway stage and the European tradition meet; the critical-edition notes record three Broadway musicals opening in 1925, the year of the Concerto's Carnegie Hall premiere; Farrington describes a writer of three-to-four-minute pop songs successfully crossing into large-scale composition; the Kennedy Center lists the Broadway shows, concert works, opera and Astaire film scores; Horowitz, relaying Larry Starr, says he moved between Hollywood and Carnegie Hall without a divided allegiance. Critics who doubted his depth (Copland's 'serious up to a point', Thomson on Porgy and Bess, the old dilettante label) did not dispute the breadth. Several independent institutions document the range, but the Library and Michigan both steward his legacy and Horowitz is an advocate, so documented at a moderate-high confidence. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): first-pass 82 / 0.66 lowered to 80 / 0.64 for admiring-source concentration (legacy custodians and an advocate); the neutral Kennedy Center and Registry sources and the critics' acceptance of the breadth keep the row high. LEAD REVIEW CORRECTION (Roster51, before eligibility, downward only): the strongest row rests on institutional and curatorial descriptions of the output (Library of Congress, Kennedy Center, Michigan editors) more than on behavioural witnesses; score and confidence lowered.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_gershwin_loc_nrr, src_gershwin_schoenberg, src_gershwin_ellington, src_gershwin_horowitz, src_gershwin_smithsonian | 1924-1937 | Registry essay + peer composer's tribute + peer composer's interview + essay-review + feature] Gilman's hostile 1924 notice (quoted by Farrington) calls the Rhapsody's tunes 'trite, feeble and conventional' yet concedes the 'rich inventiveness of the rhythms'; Bernstein (1955, quoted there) calls its themes 'terrific, inspired' while denying it is a real composition; Schoenberg's 1937 tribute calls him a great composer who contributed to the music of the whole world; Ellington (1935) calls Porgy and Bess 'grand music' that borrowed from everyone from Liszt to a kazoo band and did not use the Negro musical idiom; Horowitz sets Thomson ('crooked folklore and halfway opera'), Copland ('serious up to a point') and a dismissive 1980 New Grove entry against Heifetz, Ravel and Shostakovich; Zax says critics today are nearly unanimous that Porgy and Bess is among his finest works. The sources agree on a distinctive melodic and rhythmic gift but disagree sharply on how original and how well formed the music was, and all of them judge finished works rather than describe creative acts, so strong inference at a modest confidence. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): first-pass 74 / 0.60 lowered to 70 / 0.55 for retrospective praise (a death tribute and later retrospectives) and interpretation stronger than behaviour (critics' verdicts on works, not documented creative acts).

collaboration.rationale: [src_gershwin_loc_nrr, src_gershwin_umich_freeze, src_gershwin_smithsonian, src_gershwin_loc_symposium, src_gershwin_kennedy | 1924-1935 | Registry essay + critical-edition notes + feature + Library symposium report + Kennedy Center biography] Farrington says Gershwin wrote the Rhapsody as a two-piano score that Whiteman's arranger Ferde Grofe orchestrated page by page, and that when the clarinettist Ross Gorman improvised the opening glissando in rehearsal it pleased Gershwin; the Michigan editors say Ira made crucial contributions to Porgy and Bess and that in his early music Gershwin supplied the basic shape that singers, arrangers and producers adapted; Zax records that DuBose Heyward made fieldwork the condition of the collaboration, wrote the lyrics of 'Summertime' and took him among the Gullah community; the Library's symposium report has the composer David Raksin and other speakers saying George enjoyed helping young musicians and Anne Wiggins Brown describing her audition for him; the Kennedy Center credits shows written with Ira, other lyricists and librettists. Against this, Farrington notes that by 1927 he was unhappy with Whiteman's conducting and Nathaniel Shilkret conducted the re-recording. Concrete working arrangements are documented by several sources, but the friends' recollections and Heyward's own account are admiring and one essay supplies the Grofe and Gorman detail, so documented at a moderate confidence. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): first-pass 72 / 0.60 lowered to 70 / 0.56 for admiring-source concentration (friends' and collaborator recollections) and single-source dependence (the Grofe and Gorman details rest on Farrington).

curiosity.rationale: [src_gershwin_smithsonian, src_gershwin_loc_symposium, src_gershwin_horowitz, src_gershwin_loc_white | 1915-1934 | feature + Library symposium report + essay-review + Library curator] Zax records short Charleston stops in December 1933 and January 1934, a New York Herald Tribune report that he had become 'an eager student of Negro music', and a summer 1934 stay on Folly Island with Heyward taking him to the schools and churches of James Island to hear spirituals and the shouting dance (Heyward wrote that for him it was more like a homecoming than an exploration); the Library's symposium report says his 1915-25 piano rolls show the influence of black and Spanish rhythms and lists his 1928 meeting with Alban Berg among the influences discussed; Horowitz, an advocate, asks who among his American contemporaries so esteemed Berg; the Library's curator holds his harmony exercises and eight sketchbooks. Against this, Heyward made the fieldwork a condition and Zax says Gershwin was not known as much of a reader. Several instances of seeking out unfamiliar music at first hand, but the fieldwork was prompted by a collaborator and the characterisations come from a newspaper and an admiring friend, so strong inference at a modest confidence. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): first-pass 68 / 0.58 lowered to 64 / 0.52 for interpretation stronger than behaviour ('eager student' and 'homecoming' are characterisations, not described study) and single-journalist dependence (Zax).

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_gershwin_umich_freeze, src_gershwin_nypl, src_gershwin_loc_white, src_gershwin_loc_nrr | 1924-1935 | critical-edition notes + library finding aid + Library curator + Registry essay] The Michigan editors say the Concerto in F, commissioned in April 1925 to compose, orchestrate and perform, was the first major work he orchestrated, as he did all his later concert works and Porgy and Bess, whereas Rhapsody in Blue had been orchestrated by Grofe for a first concert work written at speed (Farrington); the New York Public Library's finding aid lists him among the students of the theorist Joseph Schillinger, with his correspondence held at the Library of Congress; the Library's curator holds his harmony exercises and sketchbooks. Against this, the same Michigan editors find that his manuscripts show impatience with notating fine detail. Three distinct signs of deliberate skill-building from independent institutions, but the self-orchestration rests on one scholarly source, the Schillinger study is an archival listing with no dates or content, and no source states his purpose, so strong inference at a modest confidence. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): first-pass 68 / 0.54 lowered to 64 / 0.50 for single-source dependence (the self-orchestration rests on Freeze) and interpretation stronger than behaviour (the Schillinger evidence shows enrolment, not a described pursuit of mastery).

detail_orientation.rationale: [src_gershwin_umich_freeze, src_gershwin_loc_white | 1925-1935 | critical-edition notes + Library curator] The Michigan editors write that his manuscripts show impatience with notating a large work in fine detail: he carefully notated pitches and rhythms but gave tempo markings, articulations and dynamics inconsistently and routinely modified details in later performances, which left later editions to supply the missing markings; the Library's curator, by contrast, calls his Porgy and Bess full score beautiful and a sign of his care, and notes song manuscripts with erasures and corrections. The two accounts pull in opposite directions (care over notes and pitches, looseness over performance markings), so the row sits near the midpoint with an inference label and a low confidence. No source gives his own working habit in his words.

adaptability.rationale: [src_gershwin_loc_nrr, src_gershwin_umich_freeze, src_gershwin_kennedy | 1924-1936 | Registry essay + critical-edition notes + Kennedy Center biography] Farrington describes a composer with about five weeks between the January 1924 announcement and the premiere, and no experience of writing a concert work, who composed a two-piano score for Grofe to orchestrate for the jazz band's players and kept the clarinettist's improvised glissando; the Michigan editors record that his shows from 1925 were book musicals rather than revues, that he moved from supplying basic shapes for arrangers to full concert scores and that he routinely modified details in later performances; the Kennedy Center says he went to California after Porgy and Bess to write film musicals. Several documented changes of format and working method, but delegating the orchestration is a division of labour rather than evidence of adjusting, and the sources describe moves between genres rather than responses to setbacks, so strong inference at a modest confidence. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): first-pass 66 / 0.52 lowered to 62 / 0.50 for interpretation stronger than behaviour (genre moves read as adaptability) and single-source dependence (Farrington and Freeze carry most of the evidence).

execution_speed.rationale: [src_gershwin_loc_nrr, src_gershwin_umich_freeze, src_gershwin_loc_symposium | 1915-1925 | Registry essay + critical-edition notes + Library symposium report] Farrington's timeline runs from the 4 January 1924 Tribune item to the 12 February premiere, with the composer also busy with a Broadway musical set to open that month and the piece written as a two-piano score for Grofe to orchestrate page by page; the Michigan editors say four Gershwin shows opened in 1924, the most of any year of his life, and that a musical in April, the Concerto in F on 3 December and two more musicals on 28 and 30 December make 1925 an extraordinary timeline; the Library's symposium report says he made 140 piano rolls between 1915 and 1925. Repeated documented bursts of output on fixed dates from two independent sources, but the pool-table story of how he learned of the deadline is told 'according to legend', the orchestration was delegated and output counts are not the pace of any single work, so strong inference at a modest confidence. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): first-pass 74 / 0.58 lowered to 70 / 0.54 for single-source dependence (Farrington and the Michigan program carry the dates) and interpretation stronger than behaviour (output counts read as speed).

provenance.notes: PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE: Wikidata wbgetentities (2026-10-16) for Q123829 returned en label 'George Gershwin', description 'American composer and pianist (1898-1937)', born 1898-09-26, died 1937-07-11, citizenship United States, ko label '조지 거슈윈'; the lead's hint was correct. SLUG/QID CHECK: no existing production or candidate file for slug george-gershwin or QID Q123829 in the roster51 worktree (data-pipeline/candidates, src/data/people, src/core). REGION: north_america, as for the existing Duke Ellington and Leonard Bernstein candidates (American composers). VOCABULARY: occupations composer, songwriter and musician, field music, impact domains artistic and cultural, tags cross_disciplinary and prolific and archetype creative_creator are existing ids used by other candidates (Ellington and Bernstein use composer, musician, music, artistic, cultural and creative_creator). PREFLIGHT RESULT: zero-politics, two or more independent perspectives, a substantive non-self behavioural source, a canonical significance source and a rights-clear portrait were all obtainable before deep research. ZERO POLITICS: no political, military or diplomatic material is scored; the Washington whites-only-theatre episode in the Library's symposium report, the Communist Party-supported framing and commentary around the 1935 interview, and the satire label sometimes attached to Of Thee I Sing are unscored and appear in no row, card or moment (the cultural debate over how Porgy and Bess portrays Black life is treated as criticism of the work, not as politics). DECEASED SUBJECT (1937): only documented public professional behaviour is scored. Excluded: family and private life (his mother, siblings, courtships and social life on Folly Island), health (the headaches and the brain tumour), his death and its aftermath, finances, painting and photography as hobbies, the Smithsonian page's linked article on a supposed attention disorder, and any inferred motive or psychology (a friend's remark that he needed approval is a psychological characterisation and is not used). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Library of Congress Information Bulletin, 'The Gershwin Legacy' (September 1998) by Raymond A. White, curator of the George and Ira Gershwin Collection (https://loc.gov/loc/lcib/9809/gershwin.html), read in full: the Library's curator calls him one of America's most important composers, who alone and with Ira wrote many of the finest American popular songs and orchestral pieces, and describes the Library's Gershwin holdings (Porgy and Bess full score, the Rhapsody in Blue, An American in Paris and Concerto in F manuscripts, sketchbooks and harmony exercises); supported by the Kennedy Center biography, the University of Michigan critical-edition release and notes (the Gershwin Initiative) and the Library's Registry essay on Rhapsody in Blue. READ (11 cited content sources plus the Library's item record and rights data and the Commons metadata): the LOC curator's article; the LOC symposium report; the LOC National Recording Registry essay by Jim Farrington; the University of Michigan concert-program notes (Freeze and colleagues) and release; David Zax's Smithsonian-magazine feature; Joseph Horowitz's essay-review; Edward Morrow's 1935 interview with Duke Ellington; the Schoenberg Center's tribute transcription; the Kennedy Center biography; the NYPL finding aid for the Schillinger papers (biographical note and scope only). All were downloaded as full text and read directly, not through a summarising tool. PERSPECTIVES: a national library's curator and its press office (legacy custodians, admiring but factual); a librarian-scholar's Registry essay that quotes a hostile critic and a mixed verdict; scholarly critical-edition editors who criticise the manuscripts; a journalist drawing on biographers and Heyward; an advocate historian who records the counter-voices (Copland, Thomson, the 1980 Grove entry); a peer composer's critique (Ellington) and a peer composer's tribute (Schoenberg); the Kennedy Center's neutral biography; and Gershwin's own words only as quoted by Zax (self; never sole support for a row). CALIBRATION: the evidence is broad on his output and working arrangements but thin on his private working habits, the institutions that describe him hold or champion his work, and most behavioural detail comes through two sources (Farrington's essay and the Michigan program notes), so no score exceeds 80 and no confidence exceeds 0.64; counter-evidence is recorded in the rows (the hostile 1924 notice, Ellington's and Thomson's criticisms of Porgy and Bess, the impatience with notated detail, Heyward's role in prompting the fieldwork, Gershwin's dissatisfaction with Whiteman's conducting). Eight rows are kept; none is padded. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): seven of the eight rows were lowered once after a re-read of the strongest rows (cross-domain range 82/0.66 to 80/0.64, creative originality 74/0.60 to 70/0.55, collaboration 72/0.60 to 70/0.56, curiosity 68/0.58 to 64/0.52, mastery orientation 68/0.54 to 64/0.50, adaptability 66/0.52 to 62/0.50, execution speed 74/0.58 to 70/0.54) for admiring-source concentration, single-source dependence, retrospective praise and interpretation stronger than behaviour; detail orientation (50/0.45) was already low and was not changed; each row's rationale ends with its own note. TRAITS NOT SCORED: persistence (the long gestation of Porgy and Bess shows commitment, but the sources describe slow progress and no documented obstacle overcome; his response to the opera's short first run is not described), discipline and deep focus (no routine documented; Zax describes slow progress and then productive months), risk tolerance (the Rhapsody commission, the Concerto and the opera look bold, but no source describes the stakes or his weighing), conflict tolerance (the critics' hostility is documented, his responses are not), independent thinking, persuasiveness, social assertiveness, leadership drive and achievement drive (his claim that Porgy and Bess was the greatest music composed in America is self-report quoted by one journalist), planning orientation, perfectionism (erasures and corrections alone do not show a standard, and the Michigan editors describe looseness over markings), aesthetic sensitivity and intuitive synthesis (praise for his melodic gift is outcome-level and overlaps the originality and range rows), impact motivation, opportunity sensing, resourcefulness and belief updating (the self-orchestration and Schillinger study could be read as responses to criticism, but no source says so). FACT CONFLICTS RECORDED: (1) the Kennedy Center says Whiteman's concerts first presented An American in Paris, which none of the other sources read describes, so the cards name the work and its 1928 date only; (2) the phrase 'lamp-black Negroisms', often attributed to Ellington, is in the interviewer's own commentary in the reprinted 1935 text, not in Ellington's quoted answers, so it is attributed to nobody in the cards; (3) the Rhapsody's start is dated from the 4 January 1924 Tribune item in the Registry essay and the card says only after the January 1924 announcement (a retelling not cited here gives 7 January from the manuscript); (4) Gilman's and Bernstein's judgments are read only as quoted by Farrington and Horowitz, not in their original publications; (5) the Registry essay finds the 1924 recording's million-seller status unsupported, so no sales claim is made; (6) the Kennedy Center counts twenty-two Broadway shows in the 1920s and early 1930s and Michigan's program counts fifteen musicals between 1925 and 1933, which are different windows, so cards use only the Michigan release's 'more than two dozen Broadway and Hollywood musicals'; (7) the Smithsonian page places a July cabin church service in North Carolina, unlike the rest of the South Carolina trip, so that episode is not used. NOT OPENED: the Library of Congress finding aid for the George and Ira Gershwin Collection (HTTP 403), the University of Michigan School of Music pages and the Gershwin Letters blog (HTTP 403), Carnegie Hall's 'Gershwin at Carnegie Hall' page (its text did not render), the Post and Courier's Folly Beach article (HTTP 429), Britannica's Gershwin biography (HTTP 403), Thomson's, Gilman's and Copland's original texts, Vernon Duke's 1947 Musical Quarterly article and Paul Nauert's article on Gershwin and Schillinger (paywalled), Howard Pollack's, Larry Starr's, Walter Rimler's and Charles Schwartz's books, Oscar Levant's and Kay Swift's recollections (not reached within the source budget), Schoenberg's 1938 written appreciation (only secondary reprints appeared in search), and the 1935 New York Times piece in which Gershwin discussed his method. Opened but not cited: Wikipedia's Joseph Schillinger article (orientation only: it gives a 1932-36 study period and a dispute over Schillinger's role in Porgy and Bess that no source I could read confirms, so no dates or role are claimed), the Berklee Today article on Schillinger, Piano Street Magazine's 2024 Rhapsody article (a retelling of Ira's suggestion of the slow theme from unnamed sources), a St. Olaf course blog, New World Encyclopedia, PBS's Broadway page, a University of Washington 1997 concert program, and All Classical Radio's Concerto in F note (secondary, citing Grove). PORTRAIT: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, George Grantham Bain Collection, item 2005678096, reproduction number LC-USZ62-60866: Rights Advisory 'No known restrictions on publication' and the Bain collection statement of no known copyright restrictions with publicity rights possibly applying (read in the Library's rights-statements data, because the Library's HTML pages are not reliably reachable); the record's own note says it contains unverified, old data from caption card, so the sitter's identification and the undated status rest on the Library's caption-card title and the Commons category (no second institutional record of this exact photograph was found; the face is consistent with the Van Vechten portraits of 1937 on a visual comparison, which is not an authoritative identification); photographer not named (Bain News Service); the Library's master TIFF is 1177 x 1536 grayscale, the same size as the Commons copy, so no larger original exists on the Library's server; saved from the TIFF, uncropped, downscaled once to 920 x 1200 (verified to open as a JPEG, never upscaled) as public/portraits/george-gershwin-bain-undated.jpg; he is shown standing, smiling slightly, in a suit. RESIDUAL RIGHTS NOTE: the basis is the Library's 'no known restrictions' statement for an agency photograph, not a licence from a named copyright holder, and the Library notes that publicity rights may apply. Considered and not chosen: Carl Van Vechten's 28 March 1937 portraits (Library of Congress LOT 12735, e.g. item 2004662906, digital file LC-DIG-ds-02793; a stronger likeness whose rights position is less clear: the Library's own statement (last revised 7 May 2024) says the donor's restrictions expired in 1986 and that the Library continues to believe the photographs are in the public domain, but records a 1998 challenge by the Van Vechten Trust's then trustee, whose stated wish is that the photographs not be cropped or colorized and that the photographer be credited), and the companion Bain photograph of him standing facing right (LCCN 2006677753, not opened at the Library).
